newsitem.title: USA: Analyst skeptical of Russia corn, soymeal imports.
newsitem.headline: Analyst skeptical of Russia corn, soymeal imports.

text.p: Russia may not import as large a volume of corn and soybean meal as Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun suggested in a speech Tuesday, a U.S.-based analyst said.

The analyst, who asked not to be identified, said Khlystun's comments appeared to be intended to please livestock producers, who have suffered under free-market reforms and are hard-pressed by meat imports.
Speaking at an industry meeting in St Petersburg, Khlystun said Russia would import four to 4.5 million tonnes of corn and soybean meal not only in 1996 but also in coming years.
"It doesn't reflect what we're expecting to happen," said the analyst, long versed in former Soviet agriculture matters.

The analyst said it was more likely wheat would dominate Russian imports. While corn and soybean meal are available, prices are high and it would be costly for the Kremlin to provide them at subsidized prices to livestock producers.
In mid August, the U.S. Agriculture Department forecast Russia would import 2.5 million tonnes of wheat and 500,000 tonnes of feed (coarse) grains.
USDA officials have said Russia would import wheat to help feed its population in the Far East.

With the introduction of the free market, the central government's main responsibility on grain purchases has been to stock food reserves and to assure sufficient supplies for the army and pensioners. The role of grain importer has been turned over to the private sector for the main part.
A decision by Moscow to import livestock feeds would be a short-term means to aid the sector, especially poultry producers, who have been hit hard by import competition.
The U.S.-based analyst noted the St Petersburg area was home to a sizable livestock industry which was reliant on grain imports in past years.

Russia has been ineligible for the major U.S. export credit guarantee programs for the past couple of years. The Agriculture Department has offered a comparatively small private-sector export credit program but it has focused on high value and consumer-ready foods and ag products.
"For significant (grain) purchases...you're talking $1 billion or so," said another U.S. analyst. "Are they going to spend foreign exchange for corn? You really have to wonder."
The analyst, who asked not to be identified, said Russia's imports would hinge more on the availability of financing than on any assessment of grain needs.
A grain industry official also was skeptical Russia had the funds or desire to make large corn and soymeal purchases.
"I can't think of any circumstances at all where they would have to import that amount of corn," said the grain industry official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The official pointed to contraction of Russia's livestock industry and to Russia's strained finances. "Money's a big part of it," he said in explaining his doubts.
For its imports, Russia probably would take wheat from Ukraine and Kazakhstan and look to Brazil, India and the United States for soymeal, the official said.
